summary:
Under Israel's threshold, wasted votes and failed coordination have repeatedly decided who could form a government. Our recount of the CEC's official files puts waste anywhere from 0.8% to 8.8% of the vote, and each high-waste election hurt one camp. In April 2019 New Right missed by 1,455 votes; had it passed, Netanyahu's bloc without Liberman would have had 61-63 seats and probably avoided the repeat election. In 2022 Meretz missed by 4,062 votes; with Meretz in, the Netanyahu bloc would have had 62 seats, and with Balad also in, 60. In 1992 the right's wasted votes gave Rabin his 61 (D7-F01 to F04).

Four regularities matter for the next two weeks.

1. Mergers rarely deliver the sum of their parts. Five of six Jewish-sector mergers since 2013 kept only 64-85% of their components' combined share; Arab reunifications are the exception. Comparative work agrees. In a Belgian ballot experiment, junior-partner supporters deserted at twice the rate of senior-partner supporters (23% vs 11%). In Finland, the penalty is concentrated in ideologically mixed lists (F08 to F11). The list deadline has passed, so this now concerns leakage inside Together, the Democrats and the Joint List, not new mergers.

2. Voters of a withdrawn or absorbed list follow their own ideology, not the leader's deal. Kolot Nodedim's polling-station estimates show only about 29% of Zehut's voters went to Likud after Feiglin's deal. About 21% of Kulanu's voters followed Kahlon into Likud, and 36-42% of New Hope's voters went to Likud after Sa'ar joined Gantz. Expect a Blue and White exit to split by ideology, with 10-20% abstaining. In the 13 October draws (whose baseline, P(NB ≥61) 12.4%, is newer than the 10 October headline), a withdrawal cuts P(NB ≥61) by 0.2-0.85 points and adds 0.2-0.4 change seats. That is worth a quiet elite arrangement, not field resources. Timing matters: Zehut's exit 19 days out removed its ballot, but Gantz's stated trigger (final-week polls) falls after the lists are published on day 9 (18 October). We found no clear rule for a later withdrawal (F12, F15, F23, F24, F27).

3. Large allies cannibalise small ones in the final weeks. Yesh Atid took about 27% of Labor's and 18% of Meretz's 2021 voters, roughly 27 times the margin that sank Meretz. Lower Saxony 2013 shows the opposite failure: insurance votes overshot and cost the senior partner power (F13, F14, F20, F21). Every change list now passes in at least 97% of draws, so the Yashar-versus-Together 'largest party' contest is cheap in threshold terms. That changes if Yisrael Beytenu or the Democrats slide toward 5 seats.

4. Surplus agreements are worth what theory predicts: at most half a seat, less as the pair grows. The two change-bloc pairs add 0.56 expected seats and cut P(NB ≥61) by 1.7 points; the Joint List-Ra'am pair cuts it by 0.7. Nothing useful is left to sign before Friday 16 October (F05 to F07, F28).

For 2026 the risks are lopsided. Expected waste falls mainly on the Netanyahu side: about 3.1 points of the vote in RZP, Amcha and Otzma failures, against 0.1 for change lists. Likud has signed with RZP and refused Otzma (F28, F29). Ra'am is the pivotal threshold list: P(NB ≥61) is 9.6% when it passes and 26.4% when it fails (F17). The Reservists list cuts both ways. Its passing lowers P(NB ≥61) (6.9% vs 14.0%), but it costs about 2.3 change seats and lowers the chance of a change-led majority, so its fate is a leadership decision (F25, F26). Polls cannot settle any of this: near-threshold Israeli lists have been mis-called in both directions (F16).

Implications for the next two weeks:
- Do not spend door-to-door field capacity on rescue.
- Tie any wasted-vote appeal to explicit coalition signals and to the final published polls by Friday 23 October (P-F25, F19).
- Monitor Yisrael Beytenu and the Democrats, and switch from 'biggest party' to bloc messaging if either weakens.
- Avoid rhetoric that depresses Ra'am's vote.
- Neither rescue nor attack the Reservists list.
- Pursue any Blue and White exit before 18 October.
- Stay silent about the Netanyahu bloc's threshold problems, which only invites insurance votes.

findings.topic: Wasted votes by election, 2019-2022, and the 2026 forecast
findings.claim: We recounted the Central Elections Committee's official locality files for every recent election, including the two 2019 elections that D1-F28's series leaves out. The wasted-vote share swings between under 1% and almost 9%. Each high-waste election hurt mainly one camp: the right in April 2019, the centre-left and Arab lists in 2022. Waste comes from two or three lists sitting within about a point of the threshold, not from micro-lists. The 2026 forecast reverses the 2022 pattern: most of the expected waste is now on the Netanyahu side.
findings.quant: Valid votes / votes for lists below 3.25% / share. Apr 2019: 4,309,270 / 366,016 / 8.49% (New Right 138,598; Zehut 118,031; Gesher 74,701). Sep 2019: 4,436,806 / 126,704 / 2.86% (Otzma 83,609 = 1.88%). 2020: 4,590,062 / 36,901 / 0.80% (Otzma 19,402). 2021: 4,410,052 / 64,752 / 1.47% (New Economic Party, led by Zelekha, 34,883 = 0.79%). 2022: 4,764,742 / 417,400 / 8.76% (Meretz 150,793; Balad 138,617; Jewish Home 56,775). 2026 (atlas share draws, 13 Oct): expected waste 5.2% of the vote (10th-90th percentile 2.0-8.6%). By camp: Netanyahu-bloc lists 3.1 points (P(above 2 points) = 0.64), unaligned lists (Blue and White, Reservists) 1.5, Arab lists 0.5, change lists 0.1.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model calculation from CEC official locality result files (Knesset 21-25) and the atlas share draws
findings.title: Wasted votes by list, 2019-2022, and expected waste in 2026
findings.venue: CEC official results; The Knesset Model
findings.relevance: This extends D1-F28 and P-F28/P-F29. The change bloc's four lists are all safe (pass probability 0.98 or higher), so its threshold exposure in 2026 runs through unaligned lists (Blue and White, Reservists) and through Ra'am. The Netanyahu bloc carries most of the waste risk (RZP-Zehut, Amcha, Otzma), which is why Likud, not the change bloc, has the stronger incentive to manage the threshold in the final fortnight.

findings.topic: 2022 counterfactuals: what the wasted votes cost in seats
findings.claim: Running the Bader-Ofer law, with the actual surplus pairs, on the official 2022 totals reproduces the actual seat allocation exactly. Meretz was 4,062 votes short. Had those votes come from Yesh Atid, the Netanyahu bloc would have won 62 seats, not 64. If Balad had also passed, the bloc would have won 60. A Labor-Meretz merger keeping every vote of both parties would have produced 62 seats for the bloc. At 80-90% retention, which is typical of Israeli mergers (D7-F08), the bloc would still have had 63. The Likud-Religious Zionism surplus agreement alone was worth one seat to the bloc, which got 63 without any agreements, and that seat came from Labor.
findings.quant: Threshold 154,855 votes. Actual Netanyahu bloc 64. Meretz passes (+4,062 votes from Yesh Atid): bloc 62 (Likud 30, Yesh Atid 23, Labor 5, Meretz 4, Yisrael Beytenu 5, Hadash-Ta'al 4). Balad passes alone (+16,784 new voters): 63. Both pass: 60. Labor+Meretz merged, retaining 100% / 90% / 80% of their votes: 62 / 63 / 63. No surplus agreements: 63 (Likud 31, Labor 5). Jewish Home's 56,775 votes all to Likud: 65.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model calculation from CEC 2022 official results
findings.title: Bader-Ofer counterfactuals for the 25th Knesset
findings.relevance: One allied list missing the threshold costs the bloc about 2 seats of margin. A merger only beats separate runs if it keeps roughly 95% or more of the parts, which Israeli mergers rarely do (D7-F08). Surplus pacts are worth about one seat across a whole bloc (D7-F07). Complements P-F28 and D1-F28.

findings.topic: April 2019: 1,455 votes decided whether there would be a repeat election
findings.claim: New Right missed the April 2019 threshold by 1,455 votes. We tested every surplus-agreement structure consistent with the actual result. In all of them, a New Right pass, with the votes taken from Likud, gives Netanyahu's bloc without Yisrael Beytenu 61 to 63 seats instead of the 60 it won. Liberman's refusal to join then led to the September 2019 repeat election. A sub-threshold list on the larger side can therefore cost that side the government itself, not just seats.
findings.quant: Valid 4,309,270; threshold 140,052. New Right 138,598 (3.22%), short by 1,455 at fixed total (1,504 if the votes are new). Zehut 118,031 (2.74%); Gesher 74,701 (1.73%). Bloc without Yisrael Beytenu: actual 60, counterfactual 61-63 (62 with Likud-New Right, Shas-UTJ, Labor-Meretz and Blue and White-Yisrael Beytenu pairs).
findings.authors: The Knesset Model calculation from CEC official results (21st Knesset)
findings.title: Bader-Ofer counterfactual for the April 2019 election
findings.relevance: This quantifies P-F29. In 2026 the analogous lists are on the Netanyahu side: RZP-Zehut (pass 0.56 in the 13 Oct draws) and Amcha (0.29). See D7-F29.

findings.topic: 1992: the right's wasted votes gave Rabin his blocking 61
findings.claim: In 1992 the threshold had just been raised from 1% to 1.5%. Tehiya won 1.22% and fell out of the Knesset. Together with Geulat Yisrael and Torah VeAretz, right-wing lists wasted about 48,500 votes. Labor, Meretz, Hadash and the Arab Democratic Party won 61 seats on 48.2% of valid votes, against 59 seats for the right on 46.8%. Our recount (no surplus agreements, which reproduces the actual seats) shows that if Tehiya's 31,957 votes had gone to Likud, the blocs would have tied 60-60 and Rabin would have had no blocking majority.
findings.quant: Valid 2,616,841. Tehiya 31,957 (1.22%), Geulat Yisrael 12,851, Torah VeAretz 3,708. Left bloc 1,260,811 votes, 61 seats; right bloc 1,225,041 votes, 59 seats. Tehiya to Likud: 60-60 (Likud 33, Arab Democratic Party 1). Under a 1% threshold: Tehiya 1 seat taken from Likud; blocs still 61-59.
findings.authors: Wikipedia contributors, compiling CEC official results; seat recount by The Knesset Model
findings.title: 1992 Israeli legislative election
findings.relevance: This is the oldest Israeli case where threshold waste flipped the bloc arithmetic, and the clearest precedent that the side with more fragmented small lists pays. Together with D7-F02 and D7-F03, it means three of the thirteen elections since 1992 had their bloc outcome tipped by wasted votes.

findings.topic: Surplus-vote agreements: the legal rule and how unevenly Israel uses them
findings.claim: Under section 67 of the Knesset Elections Law, a list may sign a surplus agreement with only one other list. Notice must reach the Central Elections Committee no later than the 11th day before election day, which is 16 October 2026. In the Bader-Ofer remainder allocation the pair counts as one list, and its joint seats are then divided between the two by the same rule (sections 81-82). An agreement has no effect if either partner misses the threshold. In 2022 all four Netanyahu-bloc lists were paired. The anti-Netanyahu side had eight lists, five at risk, and only two agreements, one of which (Labor-Meretz) died with Meretz.
findings.quant: One partner per list. Deadline: 11th day before the election. 2022: Netanyahu bloc 4 of 4 lists paired. Anti-Netanyahu side: 2 agreements among 8 lists, 1 effective (Yesh Atid-National Unity). The bloc won about 30,000 more votes than its opponents (less than one seat) but 64 seats. The Likud-Religious Zionism pair was worth +1 seat to the bloc (D7-F02).
findings.authors: Knesset Elections Law [Consolidated Version] 5729-1969, ss. 67, 81-82; Ofer Kenig (Israel Democracy Institute)
findings.title: Knesset Elections Law; The 2022 Elections: Results Analysis
findings.venue: Israeli legislation (Hebrew Wikisource consolidated text); IDI, 7 Nov 2022
findings.relevance: Each change list already has its one partner (Yashar-Democrats, Together-Yisrael Beytenu), so after 16 October no surplus lever is left. A pair between two sub-threshold lists, such as Reservists and Blue and White, is worthless unless both pass.

findings.topic: Theory: a surplus agreement is worth about half a seat at most
findings.claim: Under D'Hondt-type rules such as Bader-Ofer, two lists that pool their votes (an apparentement, which is what an Israeli surplus agreement is) can never win fewer seats together than apart. Janson's asymptotic analysis puts the expected gain for two small parties at no more than half a seat. Bochsler's Swiss data show apparentements systematically favour the larger parties. The mechanism is the D'Hondt bias toward large lists: in Schuster et al.'s exact three-party case, the largest party gains about 5/12 of a seat and the smallest loses about 4/12. A pair captures part of that large-list bonus, so the gain shrinks as the pair's combined size grows, and it is zero if either partner fails.
findings.quant: Expected gain about 0.5 seat or less (Janson 2014, citing Bochsler 2010). D'Hondt three-party seat bias without a threshold: +0.42 / -0.08 / -0.33 seats for the largest / middle / smallest party (Schuster et al. 2003). Empirical rule from our 2026 simulation (D7-F07): gain ≈ 0.5 × (1 − pair's combined share) × P(both pass).
findings.authors: Daniel Bochsler; Svante Janson; K. Schuster, F. Pukelsheim, M. Drton, N. R. Draper
findings.title: Who gains from apparentments under D'Hondt? (also: Janson, Asymptotic bias of some election methods, Annals of Operations Research 215:89-136, 2014, doi 10.1007/s10479-012-1141-2; Schuster et al., Seat biases of apportionment methods for proportional representation, Electoral Studies 22:651-676, 2003)
findings.relevance: This sets expectations: surplus pacts are about fractions of a seat. They matter in a 60-60 world but cannot substitute for keeping lists above the line, which is worth 4 or more seats.

findings.topic: 2026: what each signed surplus pair is worth
findings.claim: We ran the 13 October atlas share draws (8,000) through the seat law with and without each pair. The Yashar-Democrats agreement adds 0.36 expected seats to the pair and Together-Yisrael Beytenu adds 0.41. Together, the two change pairs raise expected change-bloc seats by 0.56. They cut P(Netanyahu bloc ≥61) by 1.7 points and raise P(change + Ra'am ≥61) by 2.7 points. The Joint List-Ra'am pair cuts P(NB ≥61) by 0.7 points. On the other side, Shas-UTJ adds 0.43 seats and Likud-RZP only 0.22, because RZP fails in 44% of draws. Together with Otzma-Amcha, those three Netanyahu-bloc pairs raise P(NB ≥61) by 0.6, 0.75 and 0.35 points respectively.
findings.quant: Baseline (13 Oct draws): P(NB ≥61) 12.4%, expected change seats 51.3, P(change+Ra'am ≥61) 26.3%. These figures are newer than the 10 Oct headline in MODEL_BRIEF_v2. Without both change pairs: 14.1%, 50.7, 23.5%. Pair seat gains: Yashar-Democrats +0.36 (theory 0.5×(1-0.248) = 0.38); Together-Yisrael Beytenu +0.41 (theory 0.42); Shas-UTJ +0.43 (theory 0.43); Joint List-Ra'am +0.36; Likud-RZP +0.22; Otzma-Amcha +0.10. All six pairs together lower P(NB ≥61) by 0.4 points net (12.8% with no pairs).
findings.authors: The Knesset Model (targeting atlas share draws; seat law with threshold, surplus pairs and Bader-Ofer)
findings.title: Marginal value of surplus agreements, 2026
findings.relevance: The change bloc has already banked its surplus value, about half a seat. The Joint List-Ra'am pair helps 'deny Netanyahu 61' about as much as either change pair does. Treat these as fixed inputs after 16 October.

findings.topic: Israeli mergers usually fail to deliver the sum of their parts
findings.claim: We compared each merged list with its components' combined share at the previous election, using official CEC shares. Five of six Jewish-sector mergers or absorptions since 2013 kept only 64-85% of the combined share. Only Zionist Union (2015) gained. Arab reunifications are the exception: the Joint List gained 15% in 2015 and 36% in September 2019, while the 2021 split lost about a third. Losses were largest when one partner was a personal vehicle or ideologically distant (Gesher, New Hope, Labor-Gesher with Meretz). This matches the comparative evidence in D7-F09 and D7-F10.
findings.quant: Likud 21.6 + Yisrael Beytenu 11.7 (2009) → Likud Beiteinu 23.3% (2013), -30%. Labor 11.39 + Hatnua 4.99 (2013) → Zionist Union 18.67% (2015), +14%. Ra'am-Ta'al 3.65 + Hadash 2.99 + Balad 2.56 → Joint List 10.61% (2015), +15%. Labor 4.43 + Gesher 1.73 (Apr 2019) → Labor-Gesher 4.80% (Sep 2019), -22%. New Right 3.22 + URWP 3.70 → Yamina 5.87%, -15% (Otzma had left URWP). Hadash-Ta'al 4.49 + Ra'am-Balad 3.33 → Joint List 10.60% (Sep 2019), +36%. Labor-Gesher 4.80 + Democratic Union 4.34 → Labor-Gesher-Meretz 5.83% (2020), -36%. Joint List 12.67% (2020) → Joint List 4.82 + Ra'am 3.79 = 8.61% (2021), -32%. Blue and White 6.63 + New Hope 4.74 (2021) → National Unity 9.08% (2022), -20%. 2026 forecasts (not results): Democrats 7.5% vs Labor + Meretz 6.85% in 2022; Joint List 7.4% vs Hadash-Ta'al + Balad 6.66%.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model calculation from CEC official results, 2009-2022
findings.title: Sum-of-parts retention of Israeli joint lists
findings.relevance: No new merger is possible now (lists closed on day 49), but the same forces act inside existing joint lists. Expect leakage from Together's smaller component and from the Democrats' Meretz wing, and do not assume a Blue and White exit or a Reservists collapse transfers as a block. Shares also move with national swing, so the causal reading is medium-confidence.

findings.topic: Who deserts a pre-electoral coalition (experiment)
findings.claim: Belgium introduced a 5% district threshold in 2003, which produced three party cartels. In a within-subject ballot experiment run during the 2004 regional campaign, students voted once on a ballot of separate parties and once on the ballot with the cartels. 89% of senior-partner supporters stayed with the cartel, against 77% of junior-partner supporters. Desertion rose with dislike of the partner, perceived ideological incongruence, a small initial party, and a favourite candidate outside the cartel. Loyalty to cartels grew over the 2003-2005 period.
findings.quant: Senior-partner supporters: 730 of 816 loyal (89%). Junior-partner supporters: 131 of 170 (77%). n = 1,255 first-year students.
findings.authors: Thomas Gschwend; Marc Hooghe
findings.title: Should I stay or should I go? An experimental study on voter responses to pre-electoral coalitions
findings.relevance: Junior components are the flight risk: Yesh Atid voters wary of Bennett inside Together, the Meretz wing of the Democrats, Balad voters in the Joint List. Retention messaging should go to those sub-electorates, not to the senior partner's base. The student sample limits generalisation.

findings.topic: Voters punish ideologically mixed joint lists (natural experiment)
findings.claim: Finnish municipal elections use open-list PR with D'Hondt and allow joint lists. A difference-in-differences design across municipalities finds that parties forming a pre-electoral coalition lose about one point of vote share and half a point of seat share. The penalty is concentrated in ideologically heterogeneous coalitions and is not significant for similar parties. D'Hondt economies of scale recover about half the vote loss in seats.
findings.quant: Pre-electoral coalition effect: vote share -1.01 points (SE 0.18; mean 17.3%); seat share -0.49 points (SE 0.21). With an interaction term: coalition × ideological range -0.73 (SE 0.29), main effect -0.43 (not significant). N = 8,081 party-elections.
findings.authors: Rafael Hortala-Vallve; Jaakko Meriläinen; Janne Tukiainen
findings.title: Pre-Electoral Coalitions: Insights into the Boundaries of Political Parties
findings.relevance: Gives a cross-national anchor for the Israeli pattern in D7-F08: a merger penalty of roughly 5-6% of combined share for close partners, and larger for distant ones. Bennett with Yesh Atid (Together) is the change bloc's most ideologically mixed list, so its retention deserves monitoring.

findings.topic: When pre-electoral coalitions form (comparative)
findings.claim: Across all potential pre-electoral coalition pairs in 20 industrialised parliamentary democracies from 1946 to 1998, coalitions are more likely between ideologically compatible parties. They are also more likely when the combined coalition would be sizeable but not too large, when partners are similar in size, and when the party system is polarised and the electoral rules are disproportional. Israel fits the pattern: the rise to 3.25% in 2014 produced the 2015 Joint List (Hadash and Balad had each won under 3% in 2013), and the 2026 Democrats and Together merged in response to the same pressure.
findings.authors: Sona N. Golder
findings.title: Pre-electoral coalition formation in parliamentary democracies (also: Pre-electoral coalitions in comparative perspective: a test of existing hypotheses, Electoral Studies 24(4):643-663, 2005)
findings.relevance: This explains why the unequal, ideologically awkward cases (Gantz with anyone in 2026, Reservists with Blue and White) did not merge. Coordination at D-14 can only work through withdrawal, surplus pacts (deadline 16 Oct) and voter-level appeals.

findings.topic: When a list withdraws or is absorbed, its voters do not follow the leader
findings.claim: Polling-station transition estimates show that voters of a withdrawn or absorbed list scatter by ideology rather than follow their leader's deal. Zehut withdrew in 2019 in return for Netanyahu's promise of a ministry, yet only about 29% of its April voters went to Likud. When Kulanu merged into Likud, about 21% of its voters followed and 46% went to Blue and White. When New Hope joined Gantz in National Unity (2022), 36-42% of its voters went to Likud. When Bennett left politics, Yamina's 2021 voters went mostly to the right, with about 11% abstaining.
findings.quant: Zehut (Apr to Sep 2019): Yisrael Beytenu 37.4%, Likud 28.6%, Labor-Gesher 14.1%. Kulanu: Blue and White 45.6%, Yisrael Beytenu 21.8%, Likud 21.0%, Labor-Gesher 12.0%. New Hope (2021 to 2022): National Unity 58-60%, Likud 36-42%. Yamina (with abstention): RZ 43.7%, Jewish Home 21.5%, Likud 13.0%, did not vote 11.1%, National Unity 9.3%. Blue and White 2021: National Unity 71-73%, Yesh Atid 30%. Estimates are constrained least squares on 6,049-9,870 common stations (R² 0.75-0.93). The 2019 matrices have no abstention category.
findings.authors: Harel Cain (Kolot Nodedim / 'Wandering Votes' project); extracted by The Knesset Model
findings.title: Kolot Nodedim: voter-transfer matrices between Knesset elections (K16-K25)
findings.venue: Open-source project using CEC ballot-box results
findings.relevance: A Blue and White exit, or a Reservists collapse, will split roughly by voters' own ideology. For these soft-right and centrist electorates, that means a substantial share going to Likud (New Hope 36-42%, Kulanu 21%) plus some abstention, whatever Gantz or Hendel endorses. This supports the model's 60/40 rescue split as a central case. These are ecological estimates, so treat them as medium confidence.

findings.topic: Labor-Meretz refusal to merge, 2022
findings.claim: In September 2022 Lapid offered Labor and Meretz reserved slots on Yesh Atid's list, plus ministries for Labor, to get them to merge. Michaeli refused. She argued that the 2020 union had cost seats and that no poll showed a merger helping. Meretz polled 4-5 seats and finished 4,062 votes short of the threshold; Labor fell from 7 seats to 4. Afterwards Meretz's leader said she had pushed for the merger and that Lapid's drive to grow Yesh Atid had drained votes from its allies.
findings.quant: Channel 12 (Sept 2022): 45% of centre-left voters favoured a merger, 35% opposed, 20% undecided. Result: Meretz 150,793 (3.16%), Labor 175,992 (3.69%).
findings.authors: Times of Israel staff
findings.title: Labor leader Michaeli rejects Lapid's incentives for union between her party, Meretz (12 Sep 2022); Meretz wiped out of the Knesset after falling just below electoral threshold (3 Nov 2022)
findings.relevance: Both sides' arguments had evidence behind them: mergers do leak (D7-F08), but one list failing cost the bloc 2 seats (D7-F02). The 2026 Democrats merger settled this. The live lesson is the large partner's final-weeks cannibalisation (D7-F14).

findings.topic: Cannibalisation: the large ally drained the small ones in 2022
findings.claim: The 2021-to-2022 transition matrix, which includes an abstention category, shows Yesh Atid drawing heavily from its near-threshold allies. It took about 27% of Labor's 2021 voters and 18% of Meretz's, roughly 73,000 and 36,000 votes. That is about 27 times the 4,062 votes Meretz eventually lacked. A further 20% of Labor's and 12% of Meretz's 2021 voters stayed home.
findings.quant: Labor 2021 (268,767): Labor 53.4%, Yesh Atid 27.3%, did not vote 19.9%. Meretz 2021 (202,218): Meretz 67.0%, Yesh Atid 17.7%, did not vote 11.6%. Yisrael Beytenu 2021: retained 73.1%, did not vote 20.0%. Based on 7,035 stations, R² 0.88.
findings.authors: Harel Cain (Kolot Nodedim project); extracted by The Knesset Model
findings.title: Kolot Nodedim transfer matrix K24 to K25 with abstention
findings.venue: Open-source project using CEC ballot-box results
findings.relevance: Within-bloc 'biggest party' appeals (D1-F25, D5-F18) are cheap in threshold terms in 2026, because every change list passes in at least 97% of draws. They become expensive if Yisrael Beytenu (6.7%) or the Democrats (7.5%) drift toward 4.5%. A rule of thumb: in the final weeks a large ally can take 15-30% of a small ally's previous voters.

findings.topic: Zehut's 2019 withdrawal: timing, procedure and result
findings.claim: Zehut filed its list by the 1 August 2019 deadline. On 29 August, 19 days before the 17 September election, it withdrew after Netanyahu promised Feiglin a cabinet post and medical-cannabis reform, and members approved the deal by about 3 to 1. Zehut does not appear in the official September results, so a withdrawal at that distance removed the list from the ballot. The deal did not deliver Zehut's voters to Likud (D7-F12). Likud's share fell from 26.5% to 25.1%, even after absorbing Kulanu.
findings.quant: April 2019: Zehut 118,031 (2.74%); Kulanu 152,756 (3.54%); Likud 26.46%. September 2019: Zehut not listed in the results; Likud 25.10%.
findings.authors: Times of Israel staff; CEC official results
findings.title: Zehut bows out of elections after Netanyahu promises Feiglin a cabinet post
findings.relevance: This is the closest Israeli precedent for a negotiated Blue and White exit. A withdrawal around D-19 cleanly removes the list, but the transfer is mostly decided by voters, not the deal. For timing limits on a late exit, see D7-F27.

findings.topic: Final polls are a poor guide to near-threshold lists in Israel
findings.claim: We compared final three-week poll averages from 2009 to 2022 with results. Lists near the line are mis-called in both directions. Lists averaging 0.5-3.5 seats survived more than half the time, and lists averaging 3.5-4.5 seats failed 22% of the time. Meretz in 2022 never polled below 4 seats in any poll after September, yet failed. Zehut (5.6) and New Right (6.1) failed in April 2019. Ra'am in 2021 averaged 1.7 seats, with most February polls at zero, and won 4. Blue and White in mid-February 2021 averaged 2.9 seats, with a third of polls at zero, and won 8. Balad in 2022 was below the line in every seat poll and came within 16,238 votes.
findings.quant: Final 21-day average versus result. Polled 0.5-3.5 seats: 44% failed (n=9; mean actual 1.9 seats). 3.5-4.5: 22% failed (n=9; mean 3.3). 4.5-5.5: 0% failed (n=9). 5.5-7.5: 9% failed (n=22). Cases (polled → won): Yachad 2015 4.0 → 0 (2.97%); Zehut 2019a 5.6 → 0; New Right 2019a 6.1 → 0; Yisrael Beytenu 2019a 2.5 → 5; Otzma 2019s 2.7 → 0; Ra'am 2021 1.7 → 4; Blue and White 2021 6.1 → 8; Meretz 2022 4.4 → 0; Labor 2022 5.3 → 4.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model calculation (polls compiled from Wikipedia's Israeli polling pages; CEC results)
findings.title: Threshold-zone backtest of Israeli final polls, 2009-2022
findings.relevance: Treat the Reservists list (4 seats in two 12 October polls, about 2.7 earlier), RZP-Zehut and Amcha as genuinely uncertain. Expect late consolidation to punish lists shown at the line (P-F30), while sectoral lists such as Ra'am and Balad tend to beat their polls. Threshold appeals keyed to polls should anticipate errors of 2-4 seats. The sample is small.

findings.topic: Ra'am: always just above the line, and pivotal in 2026
findings.claim: Ra'am has finished just above the threshold in each of its last three runs: 3.33% with Balad in April 2019, 3.79% in 2021 after polling mostly below the line, and 4.07% in 2022. On 23 September 2026 the Central Elections Committee voted 18-5 to disqualify it, and on 2 October 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously overturned that ban. Ra'am has a surplus agreement with the Joint List. In the 13 October draws its mean share is 4.65% and its pass probability 0.83. Whether it passes is the largest single threshold swing in the forecast: P(NB ≥61) is 9.6% in draws where Ra'am passes and 26.4% where it fails.
findings.quant: Ra'am-Balad April 2019: 143,666 (3.33%). Ra'am 2021: 167,064 (3.79%; final-poll average 1.7 seats). Ra'am 2022: 194,047 (4.07%). 2026: mean share 4.65%, P(pass) 0.83 (MODEL_BRIEF_v2: 4.37%, 0.78). Conditional P(NB ≥61): 9.6% if Ra'am passes, 26.4% if it fails. This is correlational: Ra'am failing coincides with low Arab turnout.
findings.authors: CEC official results; Wikipedia (United Arab List); The Knesset Model share draws
findings.title: United Arab List: electoral history and 2026 disqualification case
findings.relevance: This cross-references D2-F07, D5-F30 and the brief's exchange-rate trade-off. The change bloc does not run Arab-sector turnout work, but its rhetoric can still lower Ra'am's vote, for example by endorsing exclusion or casting Ra'am as illegitimate. The research supports a 'do no harm' line towards Ra'am. Surplus and turnout coordination is left to the Arab lists themselves.

findings.topic: Threshold insurance voting in a bloc system (Sweden 2010)
findings.claim: Fredén sets three conditions for threshold-insurance voting: the voter thinks about government outcomes, votes for a party at risk of falling below the threshold, and that party is not their first preference. Using the 2010 Swedish election study and conditional logit, she finds insurance votes for the Christian Democrats, the incumbent Alliance partner at risk under Sweden's 4% threshold. A majority of Christian Democrat voters actually preferred the larger Moderates.
findings.quant: Most Christian Democrat voters had the Moderates as their preferred party (Swedish National Election Study 2010); insurance motives are significant after controlling for party identification and left-right position.
findings.authors: Annika Fredén
findings.title: Threshold insurance voting in PR systems: A study of voters' strategic behavior in the 2010 Swedish General Election
findings.venue: Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties 24(4):473-492
findings.relevance: Insurance voting needs a declared coalition and a visibly at-risk partner (see P-F25 for Fredén's experimental follow-up). In 2026 no change ally is at risk, so insurance appeals would only apply to an unaligned list or to Ra'am, and voters treat both differently from declared partners.

findings.topic: Polls and coalition signals: strategic voting is real but a minority behaviour
findings.claim: Meffert and Gschwend ran an information-selection and voting experiment during two real German state campaigns, manipulating non-partisan polls and partisan coalition signals. Active information search gave voters fairly accurate expectations of the outcome. But strategic-voting theory explained the choices of only a minority of voters, and most insincere votes had other explanations. Coalition signals had a surprisingly strong effect on apparently strategic voting. A later survey experiment (Gschwend, Meffert and Stoetzer, Journal of Politics 79(2):642-655, 2017) finds that coalition signals raise the weight voters give to coalition considerations relative to party considerations.
findings.quant: Effect sizes are in the full text (not extracted). Strategic voting is supported for a minority of insincere voters.
findings.authors: Michael F. Meffert; Thomas Gschwend
findings.title: Polls, coalition signals and strategic voting: An experimental investigation of perceptions and effects
findings.relevance: Wasted-vote appeals to Blue and White or Reservists voters will move only a minority. Explicit coalition signals, such as who Eisenkot or Bennett would and would not sit with, move more votes than raw poll numbers. This is consistent with P-F27's estimate of about 1 in 10 Israeli voters.

findings.topic: Insurance overshoot: Lower Saxony 2013
findings.claim: In the January 2013 Lower Saxony state election, the FDP polled 3-5%, with final January polls at 4.5-5%, under a 5% threshold. Some CDU officials suggested tactical votes for the FDP, which finished at 9.9%. The CDU won 36.0%, and SPD and Greens took a one-seat majority (69 of 137). Loan votes to the junior partner overshot what was needed and cost the senior partner the government.
findings.quant: FDP polls 3-5% → 9.9% result. CDU 36.0%, SPD 32.6%, Greens 13.7%. SPD + Greens 69 of 137 seats.
findings.authors: Wikipedia contributors, compiling official state results
findings.title: 2013 Lower Saxony state election
findings.relevance: This cautions against loud 'save our ally' campaigns. Once an ally is safe, extra insurance votes are worth roughly the large list's bonus lost (D7-F06). It also explains why Likud keeps RZP at arm's length on rescue messaging, and why the change bloc should not invite insurance votes to Yisrael Beytenu or the Democrats while they are safe.

findings.topic: Germany 2013: a junior partner left unprotected
findings.claim: In the 2013 German federal election the FDP, the governing CDU/CSU's junior partner, won 4.76% of second votes and fell out of the Bundestag for the first time. The AfD won 4.70%. In total, 15.7% of second votes went to parties below the 5% threshold.
findings.authors: Wikipedia contributors, compiling Federal Returning Officer results
findings.title: 2013 German federal election
findings.relevance: This is the mirror image of D7-F20 and the German version of Meretz 2022: a senior partner campaigning for every vote can sink its ally. Together with D7-F14, it argues for monitoring Yisrael Beytenu and the Democrats in the final-week tracking polls, and for switching from 'biggest party' messaging to bloc messaging if either falls below about 5 seats.

findings.topic: Entering parliament has lasting value for a small party
findings.claim: Dinas, Riera and Roussias use the discontinuities created by national thresholds in all post-war democracies that have them. They find that entering parliament raises a small party's vote share at the next election, and that the effect is stronger in new democracies, where entry signals viability and organisational capacity.
findings.quant: Effect sizes are in the full text (not extracted). The paper estimates a causal effect of entry on next-election vote share.
findings.authors: Elias Dinas; Pedro Riera; Nasos Roussias
findings.title: Staying in the First League: Parliamentary Representation and the Electoral Success of Small Parties
findings.relevance: A threshold miss has costs beyond one election: Meretz's 2022 exit forced the 2026 Democrats merger. If the Reservists list enters in 2026, it is likely to become a lasting unaligned actor in the soft-right space Yashar and Together compete for.

findings.topic: Blue and White, 2026: the state of play
findings.claim: On 10 October 2026 Gantz said he is 'running to the end'. He rejected the wasted-vote argument, said he belongs to neither bloc, and claimed at least six seats' worth of potential voters. On 20 September he had told the Times of Israel he would halt his campaign if final-week polls showed Blue and White below the threshold. Polls have the party at about 1-2% and below the line in recent seat polls. Change-bloc leaders have pressed him to quit; Eisenkot has said that lists polling near the threshold must merge or step aside.
findings.quant: Zman Israel poll about 2% (September). Atlas draws (13 Oct): mean share 0.73%, median 0.28%, P(pass) 0.014. Gantz's 'six seats' is his own unverified claim.
findings.authors: Israel National News staff; Times of Israel staff; ynet
findings.title: Gantz refuses to quit Knesset race: 'I'm running until the end' (10 Oct 2026); Gantz to ToI: I'll drop out if I don't cross the threshold in the last week of the race (20 Sep 2026)
findings.venue: Israel National News; The Times of Israel
findings.relevance: Gantz's conditional pledge is keyed to the final-week polls, the last of which are published Friday 23 October. That may be too late for his ballot to be removed (D7-F27). A pre-agreed exit decided earlier is worth more to the bloc than a last-minute one.

findings.topic: Blue and White withdrawal: modelled effect in 2026
findings.claim: We redistributed Blue and White's share in the 13 October draws under three splits. The effect on the bloc outcome is small and depends mainly on how many of its voters go to Likud, not on whom Gantz endorses. Splits informed by D7-F12 (about half to change lists, a quarter to Likud, a fifth abstaining) lower P(NB ≥61) by about 0.4 points and add about 0.2 change seats. Only an unusually favourable split (85% to change lists) approaches one point.
findings.quant: Baseline P(NB ≥61) 12.4%, change seats 51.3. (a) 54% change / 26% Likud / 20% abstain: 12.0% (-0.4), +0.21 seats, P(change+Ra'am ≥61) +0.8 points. (b) Model's 60/40 rescue split: 12.2% (-0.2), +0.19 seats. (c) 85% change / 15% Likud: 11.6% (-0.85), +0.43 seats, +1.9 points.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model (atlas share draws, seat law)
findings.title: Blue and White withdrawal scenarios
findings.relevance: Worth a low-cost elite arrangement: no attacks on Gantz, and a dignified exit route with a role. Not worth field resources, which matches the brief's media-only rescue design. Each change list gains a few tenths of a seat.

findings.topic: Reservists-Economic, 2026: the state of play
findings.claim: The Reservists party was founded in September 2025 and runs with Zelekha's New Economic Party. It is centre-right and unaligned. It calls for a Zionist unity government without Arab or Haredi parties and does not rule out working with Netanyahu or Ben Gvir. It averaged about 2.7 seats in polls from 24 September to 7 October (Channel 13 about 3%, Walla 2.8%, Channel 14 1.8%). Channel 14 and Channel 12 polls on 12 October gave it 4 seats. It had not signed a surplus agreement as of 8 October. Its leaders' records cut both ways: Zelekha's New Economic Party won 0.79% in 2021, and Hendel withdrew Derekh Eretz from the 2022 race on 13 September 2022, before lists closed.
findings.quant: 12 Oct 2026: Channel 14 gave 4 seats (Netanyahu bloc 61); Channel 12 gave 4 (Amcha 1.8%, below the threshold). Atlas draws (13 Oct): mean 1.69%, median 0.78%, P(pass) 0.22. New Economic Party 2021: 34,883 (0.79%).
findings.authors: Israel National News staff; Keshet Neev (Jerusalem Post); Wikipedia contributors
findings.title: Two polls: Hendel and Zelekha cross electoral threshold (12 Oct 2026); Netanyahu's Likud, Smotrich's RZP sign surplus-vote agreement (6 Oct 2026); The Reservists (political party)
findings.venue: Israel National News; The Jerusalem Post; Wikipedia
findings.relevance: The list is moving up just as the final-poll window opens, so lists near the line can still move either way (D7-F16). Its stated coalition stance makes it a possible kingmaker for a Netanyahu-led or unity government. The September-October average comes from a secondary poll aggregation.

findings.topic: Reservists-Economic: why its success cuts both ways for the change bloc
findings.claim: In the 13 October draws, the Reservists list passing lowers the chance of a Netanyahu majority but also lowers the change bloc's own seats and its chance of a majority. In draws where it passes (22%), P(NB ≥61) is 6.9% against 14.0% where it fails. But expected change seats are 49.5 against 51.8, and P(change ≥61) is 3.1% against 7.4%. Forcing it above the line, with the votes taken from Yashar, Together and Likud, cuts P(NB ≥61) by 2.8 points but cuts P(change + Ra'am ≥61) by 10.4 points. A collapse with its voters split 60/40 between change lists and Likud raises P(NB ≥61) by 0.8 points but raises P(change + Ra'am ≥61) by 4.6 points.
findings.quant: Conditional on passing / failing: P(NB ≥61) 6.9% / 14.0%; change seats 49.5 / 51.8; P(change ≥61) 3.1% / 7.4%. Forced above 3.4% (votes taken 45% Yashar, 25% Together, 30% Likud): P(NB ≥61) 9.6% (-2.8), change seats 49.2 (-2.1), P(change+Ra'am ≥61) 15.8% (-10.4). Collapse 60/40: 13.3% (+0.8), 52.2 (+0.9), 30.8% (+4.6). Collapse 45/35 with 20% abstaining: 13.7% (+1.2), 52.1, 30.0% (+3.8). Brief exchange rate: +10,000 Reservists votes = change-led government +0.03 points, blocking Netanyahu +0.2 points.
findings.authors: The Knesset Model (atlas share draws, seat law)
findings.title: Reservists-Economic threshold scenarios
findings.relevance: Whether to help or hinder this list depends on the objective: it helps deny Netanyahu 61 but hurts the chance of a change-led majority, making deadlock and a repeat election more likely. That makes it a leadership decision. The research supports neither rescuing nor attacking it: attacks risk pushing its right-of-centre voters to Likud (D7-F12), and the 60/40 split is itself uncertain.

findings.topic: Legal timetable: how late can a list effectively withdraw?
findings.claim: The Knesset Elections Law sets four relevant deadlines. Lists are submitted by the 49th day before the election (s. 57(i)), approved by the 30th (s. 63), and published in the official gazette (Reshumot) by the 9th (s. 65). Ballot slips must reach polling committees at least two days before election day (s. 77(d)). We found no explicit provision on a list withdrawing after approval. In practice, Zehut's withdrawal 19 days out in 2019 removed it from the ballot (D7-F15). A final-week exit, as Gantz has floated, would come after the 9th-day publication (18 October 2026), when ballots may already be printed. If its slips stayed in the booth, residual votes for it would be wasted.
findings.quant: Day 49: submission. Day 30: approval. Day 9: publication (18 Oct 2026). Day 2: ballot slips delivered (25 Oct 2026). Surplus-agreement notice: day 11 (16 Oct 2026). Zehut withdrew at day 19 (2019) and was absent from the results.
findings.authors: Knesset Elections Law [Consolidated Version] 5729-1969
findings.title: Knesset Elections Law, ss. 57, 63, 65, 67, 77
findings.relevance: Any negotiated Blue and White exit should be timed before about 18 October to be clean. How the CEC handles a later withdrawal is an open legal question for election counsel. We could not confirm that the consolidated text is current, so check it against the CEC's 2026 timetable.

findings.topic: 2026 surplus agreements: who has signed
findings.claim: Yashar-Democrats and Together-Yisrael Beytenu signed in September. Hadash-Ta'al/Joint List and Ra'am also signed in September (D5-F30, MODEL_BRIEF_v2). Likud and RZP announced their agreement on 6 October. Likud refused to sign with Otzma, which says the refusal is designed to keep it out of a Likud-Eisenkot unity government. As of 8 October the Reservists and Amcha had not signed.
findings.quant: Deadline 16 Oct (day 11). Pairs signed: Yashar-Democrats, Together-Yisrael Beytenu, Joint List-Ra'am, Likud-RZP. Otzma: refused by Likud; an Otzma-Amcha pair is expected per the brief but unconfirmed.
findings.authors: Keshet Neev (Jerusalem Post); ynetnews
findings.title: Netanyahu's Likud, Smotrich's RZP sign surplus-vote agreement ahead of elections; Jewish Power: Likud deal designed to keep us out of Netanyahu-Eisenkot government
findings.relevance: Likud has chosen to protect RZP, which polls near the line, rather than Otzma, so Likud's final-days consolidation is likely to come out of Otzma and Amcha. That raises the chance of Netanyahu-bloc waste (D7-F29). The Shas-UTJ pair is assumed by the model but was not confirmed in these sources.

findings.topic: The Netanyahu bloc's path to 61 runs through its own small lists
findings.claim: In the 13 October draws, P(NB ≥61) is much higher when the bloc's small lists pass. When RZP-Zehut passes it is 18.3%, against 4.8% when it fails. For Otzma the figures are 15.2% against 2.5%, and for Amcha 23.6% against 7.8%. These are correlations within the draws, since lists pass on good nights for their camp, not causal effects. They still show where 'gevalt' consolidation (P-F30) would bite: votes drawn from RZP, Otzma or Amcha to Likud could push one of them under.
findings.quant: P(pass): RZP 0.56, Otzma 0.78, Amcha 0.29. P(NB ≥61) if pass / fail: RZP 18.3% / 4.8%; Otzma 15.2% / 2.5%; Amcha 23.6% / 7.8%. For comparison, change-side lists if they failed: Democrats 44.6%, Yisrael Beytenu 38.8%, Together 52.7%, Joint List 61.0% (rare events).
findings.authors: The Knesset Model (atlas share draws, seat law)
findings.title: Threshold conditionals by list
findings.relevance: The change bloc gains when the right fragments, but drawing attention to Otzma or RZP being at risk can trigger insurance votes (D7-F18, D7-F20). The research favours silence about the opponents' threshold, and attention to keeping the bloc's own allies and Ra'am above it. The strategic reading is low-confidence.

findings.topic: The 2026 threshold in votes
findings.claim: The threshold is 3.25% of valid votes, so it rises with turnout. With 7,331,981 registered voters, each extra point of turnout adds about 2,383 votes to the threshold, from about 143,000 votes at 60% turnout to about 191,000 at 80%. Using the Kolot Nodedim estimate of 4.82 million valid votes, the threshold is about 157,000. A list's survival therefore depends on its own electorate's turnout relative to the national rate, not just its poll share.
findings.quant: Registered 7,331,981; +1 turnout point ≈ +2,383 votes on the threshold; 60% turnout → about 143,000; 80% → about 191,000; valid votes about 4,823,026 (Kolot Nodedim K26 estimate) → about 156,750. 2022: 154,855.
findings.authors: Israel Policy Forum (IPF Explains); The Knesset Model
findings.title: The Electoral Threshold: What it Is and Why it Matters (24 Sep 2026)
findings.relevance: High national turnout driven by the Jewish centre and right raises the bar for Ra'am, whose share depends on Arab turnout (D2-F19, D5-F02), and for RZP and the Reservists. The change bloc's own turnout drive in liberal-urban areas slightly raises Ra'am's threshold risk, a small but real cross-effect.

open_questions: How would the CEC handle a Blue and White withdrawal announced after the lists are published on day 9 (18 Oct)? Would its slips be removed from booths? Election counsel should confirm the 2026 procedure (D7-F27).
Where would Blue and White's and the Reservists' voters actually go? No 2026 second-preference poll was found. The 60/40 split rests on 2019-2022 ecological analogues (D7-F12).

Will the Reservists list commit before election day on whom it would recommend for prime minister? Its stance determines whether its passing helps a change-led government or only blocks Netanyahu (D7-F25, D7-F26).
Will Otzma and Amcha sign a surplus pact by 16 Oct, and will Shas-UTJ be confirmed? The model assumes both (D7-F28).

How large is final-fortnight consolidation inside the Netanyahu bloc (Likud drawing from Otzma, Amcha and RZP), and does it push RZP under? This is the largest single threshold swing on that side (D7-F29, P-F30).

Do change-bloc wasted-vote appeals move Blue and White or Reservists voters in Israel today? There is no Israeli field or survey experiment; the evidence is German, Swedish and Belgian (D7-F18 to D7-F20, P-F25).
How large is the merger penalty inside Together (Bennett with Yesh Atid)? No 2026 retention estimate by 2022 vote was found beyond the 9 Sept Midgam matrix (D5-F10).

The Kolot Nodedim matrices are ecological (constrained regression on polling stations) and lack abstention for 2019. Validating the Zehut and Kulanu transfer rates against panel data such as INES would raise confidence (D7-F12).
